usage: Used to concede a point while maintaining your main argument despite that fact.
example_sentences: The weather was terrible, but even so, we managed to have a great time.
I know the price is high, but even so, the quality is worth the investment.
He hasn't had much training; even so, he plays better than the professionals.
The rules are strict, but even so, most students follow them closely.
It was a risky decision; even so, I don't regret it.
native_notes: More conversational than 'nevertheless'. It functions like 'despite that fact'.

usage: Used to introduce a point that modifies or contradicts what was just said.
common_mistakes: Starting a sentence without a previous statement
example_sentences: The project is ambitious. That said, we don't have enough budget to finish it.
She is a very talented singer. That said, she lacks stage experience.
Modern technology is amazing. That said, it has made us more sedentary.
The restaurant is quite expensive. That said, the food is absolutely incredible.
It was a logical choice. That said, I still felt a bit uneasy about it.
native_notes: Very common in natural spoken British English; implies 'having said that' in a more concise form.

usage: Used to explicitly highlight the difference between two things, people, or situations.
common_mistakes: Using without a clear subject comparison
example_sentences: My brother loves spicy food. In contrast, I prefer mild flavours.
The north of the country is industrial. In contrast, the south is agricultural.
Some companies grew last year; in contrast, ours faced significant losses.
She is very outgoing. In contrast, her sister is quite shy.
Energy prices rose sharply. In contrast, food prices remained stable.
native_notes: More formal than 'on the other hand'. Best for IELTS Writing Task 2 when comparing statistics.

uzbek: Eslatib o'taman / Shuni ham hisobga olish kerakki
usage: Used to add a qualifying or slightly contrasting remark that changes the tone of the previous point.
common_mistakes: Putting it only at the start
example_sentences: He is a bit grumpy. Mind you, he's had a very long day.
The hotel was cheap. Mind you, it was quite far from the city centre.
It was a brilliant show. Mind you, the tickets were far too expensive.
I'm feeling much better. Mind you, I still have a bit of a cough.
They have a lovely garden. Mind you, it takes ages to mow the lawn.
native_notes: Very British and conversational. Avoid this in formal essays; keep it for Speaking Part 1 and 2.

uzbek: Shu bilan bir vaqtda / Shuni ham unutmaslik kerakki
usage: Used to present two opposing facts or feelings that exist together simultaneously.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'at the same time' meaning 'simultaneously'
Using 'at the same time' as a link when the ideas don't conflict
example_sentences: Technology makes life easier; at the same time, it can make us lazy.
I love living in London. At the same time, I really miss the countryside.
It is a necessary project. At the same time, the cost is very high.
The product is high quality. At the same time, it is overpriced.
We need to progress; at the same time, we must protect the environment.
native_notes: Useful because it highlights the complexity of an issue rather than just showing one side.
russian: В то же время / Об этом не следует забывать

usage: Used to show that one action, person, or thing is chosen or happens rather than another.
common_mistakes: Using 'instead to' followed by an infinitive (e.g., 'instead of to go' instead of 'instead of going').
Omitting 'of' when a noun follows (e.g., 'I bought tea instead coffee' instead of 'instead of coffee').
example_sentences: I think we should walk to the restaurant instead of taking a taxi.
Can I have some water instead of juice, please?
Instead of studying for his exams, he spent the whole weekend playing video games.
We decided to stay at home and watch a movie instead of going out in the rain.
Why don't you call her on the phone instead of sending a long text message?
native_notes: While 'instead of' is followed by a noun or gerund, the single word 'instead' is an adverb and usually comes at the end of a sentence (e.g., 'There was no coffee, so I had tea instead.').

usage: Used to introduce a contrasting point of view, especially when weighing the advantages and disadvantages of a situation.
grammar_pattern: clause + , but on the other hand, + clause
common_mistakes: Saying 'on the other side' instead of 'on the other hand' when presenting a contrasting idea.
Using 'on another hand' which is grammatically incorrect.
example_sentences: I would love to buy a new car, but on the other hand, I need to save money for university.
Living in a big city is exciting, but on the other hand, it can be very expensive.
The job pays very well, but on the other hand, the hours are extremely long.
I want to go to the party, but on the other hand, I have to wake up early tomorrow.
Online shopping is super convenient, but on the other hand, you cannot try things on before buying.
collocations: on the one hand ... on the other hand
useful but on the other hand
native_notes: Textbooks often teach 'on the one hand' and 'on the other hand' as a pair, but native speakers in daily conversation and IELTS speaking often just say 'but on the other hand' directly to make a counterpoint.

usage: Used to connect two clauses when the second clause makes the first clause seem surprising or unexpected.
grammar_pattern: Although + clause, + clause OR clause + although + clause
common_mistakes: Using 'but' in the same sentence as 'although' (e.g., 'Although it was raining, but we went out' is a double conjunction error).
example_sentences: Although it was raining heavily, we decided to go for a walk in the park.
I managed to pass the English exam, although I didn't study very hard for it.
Although he is very young, he speaks three languages fluently.
She decided to buy the dress, although it was quite expensive.
Although the hotel was small, it was incredibly clean and comfortable.
native_notes: 'Although' is slightly more formal than 'though' and 'even though'. In spoken English, 'though' is very frequently placed at the end of a sentence instead (e.g., 'It was raining. We went out, though.').
